title: Chapter 2: Values, Types, Variables, and Expressions
description: Develop a precise value model for Java's primitives and references. The learner traces promotion, overflow, floating-point approximation, BigDecimal use, casts, equality, short-circuit evaluation, parsing, validation, and formatted output, then chooses representations that preserve a stated business rule rather than merely compiling.

lessons.title: Numeric promotion, casting, BigDecimal, and precision
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Numeric promotion, casting, BigDecimal, and precision

## Conversion happens before assignment
```java
int a = 7, b = 2;
double truncated = a / b;        // 3.0
double fractional = (double) a / b; // 3.5
long wrong = Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1; // already overflowed
long right = (long) Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1; // 2147483648
```
The declared type of the destination does not control the intermediate operation. Widen an operand before division or addition. byte and short arithmetic always promotes to int under Java's binary numeric promotion rules. Narrowing casts can discard information: (int) 3.9 is 3 and (byte) 130 is -126. Even some widening conversions lose precision, such as a sufficiently large long converted to double.

## Exact decimal arithmetic
Binary floating point cannot exactly represent many decimal fractions. For decimal business rules, use text-based BigDecimal construction:
```java
var price = new java.math.BigDecimal("0.10");
var total = price.multiply(new java.math.BigDecimal("3"));
System.out.println(total.toPlainString()); // 0.30
```
Constructing BigDecimal from a double preserves the double's approximation. Nonterminating division needs an explicit scale and RoundingMode. Rounding is a business rule: state when it occurs and whether values are rounded individually or after aggregation.

BigDecimal.equals considers scale; compareTo compares numeric magnitude, so 1.0 and 1.00 can compare numerically equal without equals returning true.

## Practice
Implement an average that cannot overflow when both int inputs are Integer.MAX_VALUE. Calculate a third of one currency unit with an explicit rounding policy, then explain why summing three rounded thirds may differ from one whole.

exercises.title: Numeric promotion, casting, BigDecimal, and precision: concept check
hints: Both operands are int, so the division truncates toward zero before the result is ever converted to double; widen an operand first if you need the fraction.

lessons.title: Operators, precedence, equality, and short-circuiting
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Operators, precedence, equality, and short-circuiting

## Evaluation and meaning
Arithmetic binds more tightly than comparison; && binds more tightly than ||. Parentheses make intent explicit even when precedence is known. Java evaluates operands left to right, but short-circuit operators may skip evaluation of their right operand.
```java
String name = null;
boolean usable = name != null && !name.isBlank();
int count = 0;
boolean selected = true || ++count > 0;
System.out.println(count); // 0
```
The null guard prevents dereferencing name. The increment is skipped because the left side of || is already true. Boolean & and | evaluate both sides, so substituting & for && can make the first expression throw.

## Equality and side effects
== compares primitive values or reference identity. Strings normally need equals for content; two separately created objects can contain the same characters without being identical. Assignment = changes a variable, while == asks a question. Prefix ++i increments before producing its value; postfix i++ produces the previous value then increments. Avoid packing several increments into one expression.

Bitwise &, |, ^, ~ and shifts manipulate integer bits. >>> shifts in zeros; >> preserves the sign bit. These operations are useful for masks and binary formats but are different from boolean conjunction. Underneath, every int and long is stored as a fixed-width sequence of bits using two's complement, which is why a negative value's leading bit is set and why -1 is all ones. A hexadecimal literal such as 0x10 or a binary literal such as 0b10000 from lesson one is simply a different way of writing the same stored value as the decimal literal 16.

## Practice
Predict `2 + 3 * 4 == 14 && false || true`, then parenthesize it. Write a safe predicate for a non-null, non-empty input. Build a decision table for “adult AND (member OR invitation)” and verify all combinations instead of testing one favorable example.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 2 assessment

Use the chapter's explanations of numeric promotion, casting, and overflow to solve the decision scenario and repair **Promotion before division**. Write a prediction of the exact decimal result before running the debugger, and preserve the intended division when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency: it checks one overflow-safe average, not every promotion and precision rule in the chapter. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for where truncation happened, then explain that tradeoff without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Chapter 2 implementation lab: safeAverage
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `safeAverage`. Return the arithmetic mean as a double without overflowing an intermediate integer sum. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Inputs may be any int values. Cast before adding or divide each operand as double to avoid overflow.
hints: Translate "without overflowing an intermediate sum" into casting an operand to double, or summing as long, before dividing by two.
Trace the public (2, 4) example plus a boundary pair such as two Integer.MAX_VALUE values and one negative/positive extreme before submitting.

exercises.title: Promotion before division
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `2.5`. The expression `(2 + 3) / 2` currently runs entirely in int arithmetic and truncates to 2 before that result is ever widened to double; preserve the demonstrated addition and explain why converting an operand before dividing, rather than hard-coding the printed value, is what restores the fractional result.
hints: Convert an operand before the division; widening the result is too late.
